bib.title: MerchantBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Long-Term Coherence in E-Commerce Operations

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: Extracted all 36 pages (99,411 chars). Read main text fully (~chars 0-30,000) and targeted the appendices (config, protocol, context management, metrics, prompts, tool tables); skimmed appendix tool/field tables and system-prompt dumps. No extraction faults except words run together in two-column text and a few table cells merged (Table 1: GPT-5.6 Sol ReAct row, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi columns glued).

SOURCE: "MerchantBench: Benchmarking LLM Agents for Long-Term Coherence in E-Commerce Operations". First author Qiming Shi (State Key Lab of CAD&CG, Zhejiang University); other affiliations: Alibaba Group (most authors, corresponding Linbo Jin, Di Weng), Zhejiang Univ. School of Software Technology, Peking University, Fudan University. arXiv 2607.28956v2 [cs.AI], 4 Aug 2026. No venue stated (format looks AAAI-style) -> preprint. Code: github.com/KhanCold/merchantbench.

CORE CLAIM: Agent benchmarks mostly use bounded tasks; MerchantBench tests "Long-Term Coherence" in a persistent 365-day seller-side e-commerce simulation (hourly steps, agent acts every 12 hours, 26 tools, 98,843 real 1688 product records, 36,576 suppliers, delayed order-level outcomes). LLM agents fall far short of humans, and trace analysis attributes this to activity decay (loss of operational coherence) and strategy drift / unrevised policy (loss of strategic coherence).

HEADLINE NUMBERS
1. Best LLM config = Qwen3.7-Max under Hermes, mean final net assets 59.46 (thousand RMB) vs Human 217.61 -> "27.3%" of human (abstract). Setup: 8 LLMs x 2 frameworks (ReAct, Hermes) x 3 runs = 48 runs; Humans = 3 participants with no prior e-commerce experience, one run each; Rule-based baseline 24.48 (3 runs). Start RMB 2,000 cash, RMB 1,000 deposit, 50 listing slots. Metric is terminal net assets (cash + deposit + in-transit + receivables), not an LLM-graded score; no pass/fail grading.
2. Under ReAct the best is GPT-5.6 Sol, 40.89; Hermes GPT-5.6 Sol 52.93. Rule-based (24.48) beats several LLM configs (e.g. ReAct DeepSeek-V4-Pro 6.56, Qwen3.7-Max 20.66, Hermes DeepSeek-V4-Pro 16.71).
3. Framework effect: averaged over the eight models, Hermes gives 53.3% higher final net assets, 71.5% higher GMV, 71.2% more orders than ReAct. Higher for 7 of 8 models (11.5% Claude Opus 4.8 to 187.8% Qwen3.7-Max); Kimi K2.6 is 4.1% lower.
4. Variance: coefficient of variation across the 3 runs is 3.3% (GPT-5.6 Sol ReAct), 10.0% (Claude Opus 4.8 Hermes) but 55.1% for the top config Qwen3.7-Max Hermes. With n=3, rankings are noisy.
5. Sustained Window Rate (min share of scheduled windows with at least one tool call across all rolling 30-day periods): Human 100%; LLMs 10.6% to 99.4% (ReAct), 17.8% to 66.1% (Hermes). Qwen3.7-Max effective window rate fell 62% to 37% (Hermes), 68% to 23% (ReAct). One Hermes Kimi K2.6 run gave up on Day 104 and took no environment action in 355 of the remaining 523 decision windows.

QUOTES
- p.1 (abstract): "the best LLM configuration attaining only 27.3% of the mean final net assets achieved by human participants."
- "Others remain active but drift from the terminal net assets objective or fail to revise ineffective policies as evidence accumulates, indicating a loss of Strategic Coherence." (Long-Term Coherence Analysis section)

LIMITS: Only 3 runs per config and 3 humans with no e-commerce experience, so no significance tests; the human baseline is tiny and not expert. Single simulated domain (China 1688 dropshipping, 10 categories); demand and risk are replayed or calibrated from real data, but customer and supplier behavior is simulated. Each model summarizes its own context (compression at 160,000 tokens, truncated to the last 30,000 in ReAct), so memory and model effects are confounded. Failure-mode accounts (Control-Loop Narrowing, Premature Abandonment, false inferences about delisting) come from representative traces, "may contribute", not controlled ablations. Frameworks differ in more than one way (Hermes adds code execution, planning, memory, skills), so the gain is not attributed to any one. No separate limitations section found. Model names (GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3.7, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4, Kimi K2.6) date it to mid-2026.

BUILDS ON: Vending-Bench (Backlund and Petersson 2025), Vending-Bench 2 (Andon Labs 2025), RetailBench (Zhang et al. 2026; 96 grocery products); tau-bench-style tool benchmarks (Yao et al. 2025); ReAct (Yao et al. 2023); Hermes agent (Nous Research 2026); POMDP formulation (Kaelbling, Littman, Cassandra 1998).

BEST-FIT NOTE SECTION: 06-evaluating-agents.md has no horizon coverage beyond RE-Bench budget curve (line 358) and SayCan. Best fit is "Agent-specific suites" (line 371), as a new row or paragraph for long-horizon/persistent-environment agents, or "Non-determinism: run every task k times" (line 262) as a counterexample (k=3, CV up to 55.1%). It does not fit Multi-turn evaluation (that is simulated-user dialogue). What the note lacks: persistent-state long-horizon eval, delayed-feedback credit assignment, activity-decay metrics (SWR), and comparison to a human and a rule-based baseline. Rule-based beating many LLMs is a useful sanity-baseline point.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.1) and Figure 2 (overview). Figure 5 (p.6; monthly effective window rate, tool calls and net profit, Human vs the eight Hermes models) best shows activity decay.

PROBLEMS: none embedded. Table 1 extraction has merged cells; values above were read from the merged text and the 27.3% matches 59.46/217.61.
